title: Garment owners weigh shutting 210 Ashulia factories without pay
excerpt: About 140 factories stopped production on 11 November. Owners decide on Saturday whether to close more under Section 13(1), which lets them stop paying wages.

image.alt: A road running past the walls of garment factories on the outskirts of Dhaka

content:
Garment factory owners have agreed to consider closing 210 factories in Ashulia and other unrest-hit areas indefinitely, The Business Standard reported on Thursday, 12 November. The decision was taken at an emergency meeting on 11 November, and a final decision is due at a members’ meeting on Saturday, 14 November.

The closures would use Section 13(1) of the Bangladesh Labour Act, which lets an employer close a factory if workers refuse to work. Workers are not paid during such a closure.

Where things stand

  • 10 November: about 146 factories suspended production, more than 100 of them in Ashulia and at least 30 in Gazipur, according to owners and Labour Ministry officials, the newspaper reported. Two workers were injured in a clash with police in Ashulia.
  • 11 November: 143 factories in Ashulia, Jamgora and Hemayetpur suspended work, owners said.
  • Already closed: three New Age group units have declared indefinite closure under Section 13(1).
  • Workers affected: about 300,000 people work in the affected belt, according to BGMEA sources.

What each side says

Owners say workers come in and mark attendance but then refuse to work, and some factories have been idle for nearly two weeks. Mohammad Rashed, vice-president of the knitwear exporters’ association BKMEA, asked how factories that had not produced for 11 days could pay wages. Shovon Islam, managing director of Sparrow Group, warned that rumours of worker deaths were spreading on social media; two workers were injured, not killed, he said.

Nazma Akter, president of the Sammilito Garment Sramik Federation, said taking to the streets “at this stage is a mistake” and urged workers to let the wage board finish its work. Workers’ representatives on the board have proposed Tk 32,000 a month; owners were given four working days from 9 November to reply.

Buyers are already moving some orders. One exporter said Marks & Spencer had shifted a large cotton trouser order to India, and the Dhaka head of a Swedish brand warned orders could fall 15% to 20% over two months, The Business Standard reported. Neither claim was confirmed by the companies.

Why it matters

Closures without pay would hit hundreds of thousands of workers and their families weeks before the new wage takes effect in December. NGOs running health, legal aid, savings or childcare programmes in Ashulia, Savar and Gazipur may see rising need for emergency support, and should plan for road blockades and field disruption. Labour rights groups will watch whether Section 13(1) is used as a lawful response to strikes or as pressure on wage talks.

What to watch

  • The owners’ decision on Saturday, 14 November.
  • The owners’ counter-proposal to the wage board and the board’s next meeting.
  • Any intervention by the Labour Ministry on the use of Section 13(1).
